Built through self-supervision on large, diverse datasets, GMAI will flexibly interpret different combinations of medical modalities, including data from imaging, electronic health records, laboratory results, genomics, graphs or medical text. Models will in turn produce expressive outputs such as free-text explanations, spoken recommendations or image annotations that demonstrate advanced medical reasoning abilities. Here we identify a set of high-impact potential applications for GMAI and lay out specific technical capabilities and training datasets necessary to enable them. We expect that GMAI-enabled applications will challenge current strategies for regulating and validating AI devices for medicine and will shift practices associated with the collection of large medical datasets. This review discusses generalist medical artificial intelligence, identifying potential applications and setting out specific technical capabilities and training datasets necessary to enable them, as well as highlighting challenges to its implementation.

papers.title: Biologically informed deep learning to query gene programs in single-cell atlases
papers.abstract: Abstract The increasing availability of large-scale single-cell datasets has enabled the detailed description of cell states across multiple biological conditions and perturbations. In parallel, recent advances in unsupervised machine learning, particularly in transfer learning, have enabled fast and scalable mapping of these new single-cell datasets onto reference atlases. The resulting large-scale machine learning models however often have millions of parameters, rendering interpretation of the newly mapped datasets challenging. Here, we propose expiMap, a deep learning model that enables interpretable reference mapping using biologically understandable entities, such as curated sets of genes and gene programs. The key concept is the substitution of the uninterpretable nodes in an autoencoder’s bottleneck by labeled nodes mapping to interpretable lists of genes, such as gene ontologies, biological pathways, or curated gene sets, for which activities are learned as constraints during reconstruction. This is enabled by the incorporation of predefined gene programs into the reference model, and at the same time allowing the model to learn de novo new programs and refine existing programs during reference mapping. We show that the model retains similar integration performance as existing methods while providing a biologically interpretable framework for understanding cellular behavior. We demonstrate the capabilities of expiMap by applying it to 15 datasets encompassing five different tissues and species. The interpretable nature of the mapping revealed unreported associations between interferon signaling via the RIG-I/MDA5 and GPCRs pathways, with differential behavior in CD8 + T cells and CD14 + monocytes in severe COVID-19, as well as the role of annexins in the cellular communications between lymphoid and myeloid compartments for explaining patient response to the applied drugs. Finally, expiMap enabled the direct comparison of a diverse set of pancreatic beta cells from multiple studies where we observed a strong, previously unreported correlation between the unfolded protein response and asparagine N-linked glycosylation. Altogether, expiMap enables the interpretable mapping of single cell transcriptome data sets across cohorts, disease states and other perturbations.

papers.title: ProteinBERT: a universal deep-learning model of protein sequence and function
papers.abstract: SUMMARY: Self-supervised deep language modeling has shown unprecedented success across natural language tasks, and has recently been repurposed to biological sequences. However, existing models and pretraining methods are designed and optimized for text analysis. We introduce ProteinBERT, a deep language model specifically designed for proteins. Our pretraining scheme combines language modeling with a novel task of Gene Ontology (GO) annotation prediction. We introduce novel architectural elements that make the model highly efficient and flexible to long sequences. The architecture of ProteinBERT consists of both local and global representations, allowing end-to-end processing of these types of inputs and outputs. ProteinBERT obtains near state-of-the-art performance, and sometimes exceeds it, on multiple benchmarks covering diverse protein properties (including protein structure, post-translational modifications and biophysical attributes), despite using a far smaller and faster model than competing deep-learning methods. Overall, ProteinBERT provides an efficient framework for rapidly training protein predictors, even with limited labeled data. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: Code and pretrained model weights are available at https://github.com/nadavbra/protein_bert. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

papers.title: Learning Protein-Protein Interaction Interfaces from Multimodal Representations
papers.abstract: Background: Protein-protein interactions govern essential cellular processes, making the identification of interface residues critical for protein engineering and molecular design. Although complex deep learning algorithms like AlphaFold3 generate full atom resolution assemblies, they are not optimized for residue-level interface identification. Existing methods face inherent limitations: sequence-based models lack explicit 3D context, while structure-based approaches can overlook evolutionary signals. Results: By combining evolutionary context with 3D geometry, the multimodal protein language model ESM3 offers the ideal foundation for residue-level interface classification. This results in the ESM3-PPISites model, which outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods across diverse training and benchmark sets. Generalization is assessed through stringent sequence- and structure-based redundancy filtering to ensure evaluation on previously unseen proteins. Notably, finetuning the open-weight ESM3 architecture meaningfully narrows the performance gap with its proprietary full-scale counterpart. Furthermore, integrating predicted interaction sites as spatial restraints into HADDOCK significantly improves the recovery of near-native binding poses while reducing computational search time by an order of magnitude compared with blind docking. Conclusions: ESM3-PPISites enables accurate interfaces identification without relying on complex structural inputs at inference time, establishing a reliable and computationally efficient strategy for mapping protein-protein interaction sites.

papers.title: hvantk: an agentic multi-omics framework for variant annotation and analysis
papers.abstract: Large-scale genetic variant analysis involves multiple computational steps, data formats, gene and variant annotation sources and compute requirements. Some of the steps like joint calling for large cohorts are run on large compute clusters, while gene/variant classification algorithms can be run in a desktop computer. At the same time, variant annotations such as gene expression and gene constraints metrics from gnomAD are provided in different formats, by resources that frequently change their versions. Here, we present hvantk, a framework that provides a common data model for large-scale annotation and analysis of genetic variants, by extending popular data formats such as Hail MatrixTable and AnnData. hvantk agentically integrates 21 public multi-omic data providers as plugins that a developer, bioinformatician or an AI agent can author without modifying the framework's core, drives analysis workflows using agent skills, and scales from single desktop computers to high-performance computing clusters. We used hvantk for reanalysing three case-control cohorts, comprising congenital heart disease (CHD), developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (Epi25) and schizophrenia (SCHEMA). Re-ranking of gene-based burden testing results using multi-omic annotations improved the recovery of curated disease genes from 26% to 49% in CHD, 40% to 48% in Epi25 and 51% to 54% in SCHEMA, among the top decile re-ranked genes. Expression at bulk and single-cell levels were the features contributing the most over a baseline of burden, gene constraint and publication count.

papers.title: MADDIE: Multi-Agent Drug Discovery Engine
papers.abstract: Drug discovery remains a resource-intensive and time-consuming process, involving billions of dollars and a decade of development to advance a drug to market. While many in silico tools have accelerated this process, operating them still demands substantial time, effort, and expertise from medicinal chemists. Autonomous systems built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a promising solution, yet current designs limit their performance. Existing single-agent systems scale poorly to long-horizon, multi-step, and realistic tasks, whereas multi-agent systems typically execute predefined workflows that cannot capture the iterative, non-linear nature of a real drug discovery campaign. Here, we present MADDIE, a multi-agent drug discovery engine. It comprises a central agent, Orchestrator, and four specialized worker agents: HitIdentifier, LeadOptimizer, Synthesizer, and Evaluator, each representing a critical step in a drug discovery campaign. Under Orchestrator's orchestration and coordination, these worker agents are composed into flexible workflows, enabling MADDIE to adapt its strategy and navigate the drug discovery pipeline end-to-end. Across 50 protein targets, MADDIE produces molecules satisfying key property requirements and their synthesis routes, outperforming existing agentic systems, generative models, and general-purpose LLMs by a wide margin. Our analysis reveals how these agents collaborate and that MADDIE can employ different strategies across targets to achieve the campaign's goal, while still being efficient in time and tokens. Together, they demonstrate MADDIE as a low-cost, effective, and efficient autonomous engine for accelerating drug discovery. Code and dataset is available via https://github.com/ninglab/MADDIE.

papers.title: Multimodal contrastive learning for spatial gene expression prediction using histology images
papers.abstract: In recent years, the advent of spatial transcriptomics (ST) technology has unlocked unprecedented opportunities for delving into the complexities of gene expression patterns within intricate biological systems. Despite its transformative potential, the prohibitive cost of ST technology remains a significant barrier to its widespread adoption in large-scale studies. An alternative, more cost-effective strategy involves employing artificial intelligence to predict gene expression levels using readily accessible whole-slide images stained with Hematoxylin and Eosin (H&E). However, existing methods have yet to fully capitalize on multimodal information provided by H&E images and ST data with spatial location. In this paper, we propose mclSTExp, a multimodal contrastive learning with Transformer and Densenet-121 encoder for Spatial Transcriptomics Expression prediction. We conceptualize each spot as a "word", integrating its intrinsic features with spatial context through the self-attention mechanism of a Transformer encoder. This integration is further enriched by incorporating image features via contrastive learning, thereby enhancing the predictive capability of our model. We conducted an extensive evaluation of highly variable genes in two breast cancer datasets and a skin squamous cell carcinoma dataset, and the results demonstrate that mclSTExp exhibits superior performance in predicting spatial gene expression. Moreover, mclSTExp has shown promise in interpreting cancer-specific overexpressed genes, elucidating immune-related genes, and identifying specialized spatial domains annotated by pathologists. Our source code is available at https://github.com/shizhiceng/mclSTExp.

papers.title: Identification of gene kinetics patterns improves RNA velocity and cell fate prediction using JuloVelo
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA velocity has transformed our capacity to predict future cell states from sequencing snapshots, but existing methods rely on constant or binary kinetic assumptions that fail to capture the heterogeneous splicing dynamics of cellular differentiation. Here we present JuloVelo, a deep learning framework that demonstrates that identifying gene kinetics patterns to initialize neural network training dramatically improves RNA velocity model performance. By pre-determining whether each gene follows a Circle, Complete induction, or Complete repression pattern across cellular differentiation, JuloVelo initializes training with pattern-matched, pre-trained network weights, effectively guiding the cell-specific kinetics optimization away from biologically implausible parameter regimes. Additionally, JuloVelo demonstrates that multiome datasets can also be processed and modeled by utilizing promoter chromatin accessibility to guide kinetics pre-determination, and integrates an in silico perturbation framework to simulate transcription factor modulation on cell fate. Validated across eight datasets spanning erythrogenesis, neurogenesis, and endocrinogenesis, JuloVelo consistently outperformed constant-rate and cell-specific models, resolving the entire five-lineage differentiation program in hippocampal neurogenesis. Multiome processing improved both intrinsic and extrinsic velocity stability, and JuloVelo reduced computational execution time by approximately 70% compared to cellDancer. JuloVelo is available as an open-source package at https://github.com/jhlabtw/JuloVelo.jl.

papers.title: recAMPLIFY: Large-Scale Pretraining of Recursive Protein Language Models
papers.abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) are powerful tools for protein annotation and mutation-effect prediction, but progress has largely depended on scaling model size and data, making them expensive and prone to memorization. Test-time scaling offers a complementary path, but methods developed for autoregressive LLMs do not transfer directly: masked encoders lack a generation loop, and amino acids do not verbalize in a reasoning language. Instead, we adapt recursive pretraining to masked pLMs, where a weight-tied Transformer core refines residue-aligned hidden states over an adjustable number of cycles. We instantiate this recipe as recAMPLIFY, a pLM with 155M unique parameters trained on the same 2T tokens as AMPLIFY-350M. Despite 56% fewer parameters, it improves CASP contact recovery and three out of four supervised tasks, notably raising fold accuracy by 22.5%. Because optimal depth for recAMPLIFY varies across tasks and assays, we then introduce Gated Mixture Recurrence (GMR), a framework that decodes each protein from a probability-weighted mixture of hidden states visited during recursion. GMR employs a learned residual gate at scalar, low-rank, or per-dimension resolution to control how much of each cycle's proposed update is accepted into the state. This unifies halting and gating into a single adaptive computation objective while recovering PonderNet-style halting as a special case without gates. Layered on top of recAMPLIFY, GMR further reduces expected layer depth by up to 37%, although the accuracy trade-off varies by task. Mechanistic analyses show that residual gating controls recurrence stability beyond the trained depth and that halt depth tracks biological properties.

papers.title: On the Selectivity of Generative Models in Structure-Based Drug Design
papers.abstract: Designing small-molecule drugs that selectively bind to a target protein while avoiding unintended interactions with other proteins is essential for reducing side effects that contribute substantially to clinical attrition. Although structure-based drug design (SBDD) has advanced rapidly with deep learning, most generative models still optimize binding to a single target and disregard selectivity due to limited training data and unknown off-target interactions. Motivated by this gap, we introduce SELECTBENCH, a comprehensive benchmark assessing the selectivity of generative SBDD models. SELECTBENCH provides three curated evaluation tasks reflecting different real-world drug discovery scenarios: literature-based case studies, safety screening panels used in pharmaceutical development, and large-scale structure-based evaluation sets. We further introduce a suite of metrics to quantify selectivity and conduct a systematic evaluation of nine representative SBDD models, including methods explicitly trained for selectivity and widely-used inference-time guidance techniques. Our results show that even selectivity-trained models achieve only modest off-target discrimination and inference-time guidance provides limited gains, underscoring the need for method improvement. SELECTBENCH provides both a characterization of where current generative SBDD stands on selectivity and an open, extensible platform to accelerate progress. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/lovetaro/selectbench.

papers.title: Do LLM Proposers Improve Budgeted Search for Ionizable Lipids?
papers.abstract: Efficient lipid design under limited experimental budgets is a central challenge in computational chemistry and drug discovery. We introduce LEAF (Lipid Evolutionary Adaptive Framework), a matched-budget protocol for testing whether language-model proposers improve combinatorial molecular search relative to classical baselines. The study uses a 30,044-candidate ionizable-lipid space, a frozen Gaussian-process oracle fitted to experimental potency labels, and a separate active-learning surrogate. Four language models evaluated over eight seeds and three splits show no significant improvement over genetic-algorithm or random-search baselines. For Llama 8B, 79.1% of acquisition-selected queries repeat previously evaluated archive members. Removing duplicates reduces the performance gap on some splits but increases proposal cost and can prevent budget exhaustion. Larger models reduce duplication without establishing superiority or equivalence. Exploratory scored prompts and stricter novelty controls yield positive median differences against the genetic algorithm, yet wide intervals and shared-seed dependence preclude stronger conclusions. A validated single-assay reanalysis preserves the chemotype-cold deficit at a smaller numerical scale, and exploratory expected hypervolume improvement does not reverse the result. Follow-up checks address whether proposers genuinely use injected evidence. These checks include a zero-shot leakage probe, rank-only and chain-of-thought-rationale prompts, a score-shuffle perturbation, an evidence-conflict probe, and a genuine reasoning-mode proposer. They show measurable engagement with supplied information without a corresponding performance gain. LEAF isolates proposal quality as the experimental variable and documents a concrete failure mode of zero-shot LLM proposers under controlled budgets.

papers.title: DMAIC-Bench: From Self-Reflection to Self-Restraint for Agents in Multi-Stage Analytical Tasks
papers.abstract: Multi-stage analytical tasks require LLM agents to use intermediate evidence to decide whether to continue, redirect or stop. Self-reflection, in which an agent critiques its output, is widely studied, yet a critique does not show whether evidence changed the next action. We call that capability self-restraint. Existing agent benchmarks largely measure task completion or output quality and leave it untested. DMAIC-Bench evaluates it with 97 seeded tasks across 15 industrial cases in four sectors, built around Lean Six Sigma's explicit statistical prerequisites. Paired counterfactual variants require opposite actions at the same workflow position, distinguishing warranted restraint from indiscriminate stopping. We assess execution traces with a private scorer and final claims through independent expert review. Across 13 models from six providers, execution-level routing accuracy averages 92% on matched GO decisions and 19% on NO-GO decisions, counting any forbidden downstream computation as a route error. Execution traces show agents reporting correct diagnostics before performing analyses that those results disallow. Separately, blinded expert review of the 11 audited agents estimates that reports act on invalid evidence at 47% of reached NO-GO decisions, with an interval from 31% to 61%. Explicit stopping permission helps some models without consistently restoring correct decisions at both GO and NO-GO forks. Sixteen life-sciences tasks in bulk ribonucleic acid sequencing (RNA-seq) and case-control genome-wide association studies (GWAS) show that the same framework can evaluate evidence-dependent decisions beyond industrial workflows. Project code and data are available at: https://github.com/psptpx/DMAIC-Bench-public.

papers.title: Human Islet Transcriptomics in Type 2 Diabetes Reveals Conserved Dysfunction Axes and a Candidate Gene Panel
papers.abstract: Background. Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D) involves progressive pancreatic beta-cell dysfunction, but conserved islet programs require cross-cohort and single-cell validation. Methods. We integrated four human islet transcriptomic cohorts using differential expression, random-effects meta-analysis, Hallmark scoring, and module scoring. To test generalizability without reusing held-out outcomes, modules were re-derived from three cohorts and scored in the fourth in rotating study-level cross-fitting, with expression- and detection-matched random gene-set nulls. Machine-learning performance in GSE164416 was estimated by nested stratified 5-fold cross-validation with DEG calling and feature selection repeated within each outer training fold. An annotation-compatible score was tested in GSE50244, and beta-cell validation used GSE221156. Results. Cross-fitted IsletDysfunctionScore effects were positive in all four held-out cohorts (d = 0.39-1.36; pooled Hedges g = 0.905, 95% CI 0.501-1.309, p = 1.14 x 10^-5, I2 = 5.5%). Matched gene-set null testing supported effects beyond random expectation in two cohorts. Nested machine learning yielded AUC = 0.960 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.900-0.997); GABRA2 and ENSG00000284653 were selected in all outer folds. The external 8-gene consensus-pool score achieved AUC = 0.907 (DeLong 95% CI 0.818-0.996), but its fixed threshold did not transfer. In GSE221156, the single-cell dysfunction-score analog increased and BetaIdentitySecretion decreased in T2D; ImmuneStress was nominally increased but did not survive false-discovery correction across the single-cell score family. Conclusions. Human T2D islets show a reproducible stress/identity-loss framework that generalizes directionally under study-level cross-fitting and beta-cell-resolved validation. The candidate panel is a research transcriptomic signature requiring further validation.

papers.title: CAPO: Compute-Aware Automated Protein-Model Optimization
papers.abstract: Protein models such as Evolutionary Scale Modeling (ESM), AlphaFold and Boltz have transformed computational protein science, yet a pretrained model rarely transfers to a particular laboratory's assay without adaptation to its data and experimental setting, and that adaptation is technically demanding and spends real compute budget. Existing agentic systems can automate model training, yet typically treat fine-tuning as a reliable tool call: feasibility and cost are estimated rather than measured, and infeasibility is discovered only after compute has been spent. We formulate protein-model adaptation as a gated decision problem: given a task, raw data and a compute budget c_max, a system should decide whether and how to adapt a model before committing expensive computation. We introduce CAPO (Compute-Aware Automated Protein-Model Optimization), a multi-agent system built around one rule: gate before you train. CAPO measures feasibility on the target accelerator, projects cost against the available budget, runs a canary inside the actual training loop and maintains an auditable artifact trail; critically, it can decline an unaffordable adaptation and select a cheaper alternative. We evaluate CAPO, without system changes, on three protein-modeling tasks: (i) SARS-CoV-2 host-range prediction, (ii) hit-to-lead affinity ranking and (iii) temporal variant-effect reclassification. On host range, CAPO partially fine-tuned an 8-million-parameter ESM-2 model to a species-averaged MCC of 0.826, compared with 0.743 for a hand-designed expert transformer; it matched a general coding agent while using 57.4% less GPU time and reduced failed training trials from four to zero. For hit-to-lead affinity ranking, CAPO rejected Boltz-2 fine-tuning and instead trained an assay-calibrated lightweight head over frozen representations, improving ranking on 11 of 15 held-out targets in 1.68 GPU-hours. On temporally held-out ClinVar variants, rank-4 low-rank adaptation of ESM-2 reached an MCC of 0.478, compared with 0.252 for a one-hot baseline and 0.000 for the frozen zero-shot score. These results come from single runs, without a gate ablation and with one generalist-agent comparison. Within those limits, they show that measured admission control can make protein-model adaptation not only automated but selective: deciding what to compute, what not to compute and why.

papers.title: Boundary Detection for High-Dimensional Point Clouds
papers.abstract: We introduce two new methods for boundary detection in high-dimensional point cloud data, intended to work in situations with non-uniform density, high ambient dimension, and substantial noise. Our first method fits a separating hyperplane on local neighborhoods after doing local dimension reduction---this method works best when one can reliably estimate the intrinsic dimension of the data. Our second method measures the directional uniformity of local neighborhoods, and has the best overall performance on synthetic data. In addition to pointwise numerical boundary scores, our algorithms yield an estimated normal vector at each boundary point. We validate our methodology on synthetic data as well as two real examples: we analyze spatial transcriptomics data, where we show that we can detect the boundary of a tumor, and we also study LLM activation geometry.

papers.title: Generative modeling of spatially resolved perturbation responses with CONCERT
papers.abstract: Spatial perturbation transcriptomics measures gene expression responses to genetic or chemical perturbations in intact tissue. Each response depends on the intrinsic state of a cell and on its niche, the neighboring cells through which perturbation effects propagate. Here we present CONCERT a niche-aware Gaussian process variational autoencoder that embeds each perturbation with the niche of the receiving cell and learns a spatial kernel for each perturbation, whose lengthscale sets how far the effect extends in tissue. We evaluate CONCERT in within-niche prediction, for held-out cells in the niche where a perturbation was measured, and in cross-slide prediction, for a slide from which the perturbation was withheld during training. On a SPAC-seq screen of hundreds of knockouts at single-cell resolution and on Perturb-map lung tumors at spot resolution, CONCERT predicts response magnitude and gene ranking more accurately than counterfactual models trained on dissociated cells, spatial perturbation models and spatial nearest neighbor aggregation. In dextran sodium sulfate colitis, where each mouse is sampled once, CONCERT reconstructs spatial gene expression at unmeasured time points, enabling longitudinal comparison that separates changes over time from differences between mice. The predictions recover the nonmonotonic course of injury, which peaks at day 9 and resolves by day 21. In ischemic stroke, CONCERT predicts responses to lesions of different sizes and locations, in single sections and across serial sections in three dimensions, and reproduces the expression patterns of the lesion core and perilesional tissue. Across lung tumor, colon and brain tissue, CONCERT predicts niche-aware counterfactual responses at locations where a perturbation was not measured and reconstructs missing spatial data.

papers.title: SpaCEy links spatial tissue patterns to clinical outcomes using explainable graph neural networks.
papers.abstract: Tissues are complex ecosystems organised in space, and alterations in this organisation underpin multiple diseases. Spatial omics enables molecular profiling of tissue organisation, but linking these patterns to clinical outcomes remains challenging. We present SpaCEy (Spatial Clinical Explainability), an explainable graph neural network that identifies tissue patterns predictive of clinical outcomes in spatial proteomics datasets. SpaCEy models tissues as spatial graphs from molecular marker expression, without using predefined cell-type labels or anatomical regions as model inputs. Its embeddings capture intercellular relationships and molecular dependencies for predicting overall survival and disease progression. An integrated explainer identifies recurring spatial patterns and coordinated marker expression relevant to model predictions. Applied to a spatial proteomic lung cancer cohort, SpaCEy identifies spatial and protein-expression patterns associated with disease progression. Across multiple breast cancer proteomic datasets, it stratifies patients by overall survival, both across and within established clinical subtypes, and highlights protein markers underlying this stratification.

papers.title: GLM-Prior: a genomic language model for transferable sequence-derived priors in gene regulatory network inference.
papers.abstract: Gene regulatory network inference depends on high-quality prior knowledge, yet curated priors are often incomplete or unavailable across species and cell types. We present GLM-Prior, a genomic language model fine-tuned to predict transcription factor-target gene interactions from nucleotide sequence. We integrate GLM-Prior with PMF-GRN in a dual-stage pipeline that combines sequence-derived priors with single-cell expression data for prior-conditioned GRN inference. Across six cell-line contexts, GLM-Prior performance scales with positive label abundance and TF coverage, showing above-chance agreement with reference networks in well-annotated mammalian settings. Single-species, species-transfer, and multi-species training show that GLM-Prior can construct informative priors across related mammalian species. Compared with accessibility-based priors, GLM-Prior achieves the highest prior performance in four of five mammalian cell lines. These benchmarks show that prior quality largely constrains GRN inference performance, positioning GLM-Prior as a transferable workflow for sequence-derived prior construction when matched experimental assays are unavailable.

papers.title: Regulatory-prior-guided attention preserves biological structure during unpaired single-cell RNA-ATAC integration.
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing and single-cell ATAC sequencing provide complementary views of transcriptional output and chromatin regulatory potential, but integrating unpaired profiles remains challenging because the modalities differ in feature space, sparsity and noise. Existing approaches often frame integration as distribution matching, which can over-align biologically distinct, condition-specific or modality-specific cell states. We present scHPGT, a single-cell Heterogeneous Prior-Guided Transformer for regulatory-prior-guided integration of unpaired RNA and chromatin accessibility profiles. scHPGT uses modality-specific encoders to model RNA and ATAC signals, a prior-guided cross-modal Transformer to constrain gene-peak attention using regulatory links, and a domain-adversarial objective to reduce modality-specific discrepancies in a shared latent space. Across PBMC3k, mouse spleen, CITE-seq/ASAP-seq PBMC and PBMC10k benchmarks, scHPGT improves clustering agreement, label transfer and biological structure preservation while maintaining effective modality alignment. In partial-overlap and condition-shift settings, scHPGT aligns shared populations without forcing unmatched or condition-specific states into inappropriate correspondence. Attention-derived links recover regulatory relationships, highlight marker-gene regulatory regions, recover transcription factor programs and produce regulatory activity profiles consistent with cell-type-specific transcriptional programs. Code and datasets are released at https://github.com/zlCreator/scHPGT.

papers.title: Mechanisms Matter: Transportability of Cellular Perturbation Effects
papers.abstract: Predicting cellular responses to perturbations across biological contexts is central to drug development, yet deep learning models often fail to outperform simple baselines. Leveraging causal transportability theory, we show that cross-context generalization is governed by shared causal mechanisms, not merely distributional similarity. To enable controlled evaluation, we develop a causal simulator that generates realistic semi-synthetic Perturb-seq datasets with tunable mechanistic divergence, providing benchmarks with known ground-truth causal structure. Further, we adapt the Vendi score to the perturbation setting to quantify effective response diversity and diagnose mode collapse, a failure mode invisible to standard per-perturbation metrics. Extensive experiments across six deep learning models and five simple baselines on semi-synthetic and real Perturb-seq datasets reveal a cross-context generalization gap: performance under cross-context splits drops substantially, often to simple baseline levels. Notably, even on synthetic data with fully specified causal structure, no model generalizes across contexts with different causal mechanisms. Across real and semi-synthetic datasets, lower cross-context concordance of transcriptome-wide impact tracks larger transfer gaps, providing an empirical proxy for perturbation-relevant mechanistic divergence. Code is available at https://github.com/microsoft/mechanisms_matter.

papers.title: Filling the Missing Puzzle: Integrating Interaction and Evolutionary Information to Enhance Protein Fitness Prediction in Inverse Folding
papers.abstract: Protein inverse folding, which infers compatible amino acid sequences from a given backbone structure, is central to rational protein design. Current methods rely largely on sequence recovery rate as the evaluation metric, emphasizing structural compatibility but seldom addressing function. Yet functional activity depends on the proper network of non-covalent interactions-protein-ligand contacts being a prime example. We argue that function-oriented protein design is governed by three complementary constraints: structural, interaction, and evolutionary, none of which are handled in a unified manner by existing pretrained models. To bridge this gap, we introduce zPolaron, a graph neural network built on protein-ligand complexes for functional protein design. zPolaron represents residues and ligand atoms as a heterogeneous graph and jointly encodes structural, interaction, and evolutionary information by fusing physical-interaction-enhanced graph representations with ESM-2 embeddings. Across multiple fitness prediction benchmarks, zPolaron outperforms all baselines, with gains evident across structural, interaction, and evolutionary dimensions. Wet-lab experiments further confirm its utility in functional enzyme screening and design: the optimized CalA6-D205A-S160G mutant achieves a 17.84-fold improvement in activity, while the CalB-I121M mutant yields a 1.91-fold increase. Together, these results show that integrating interaction and evolutionary information fills the missing puzzle of inverse folding, enhancing protein fitness prediction beyond structural compatibility. zPolaron is available at https://github.com/zelixirSH/zPolaron.

papers.title: Reformulating Protein Corona Prediction as Universal Protein-conditioned Learning
papers.abstract: When nanoparticles enter biological environments, their surfaces are rapidly coated by proteins, forming a protein corona that governs their biological identity and downstream responses. Existing computational methods treat each protein as an independent prediction task, preventing the learning of shared adsorption principles and limiting generalization beyond experimentally characterized proteins. Here we introduce NanoPCT, a universal protein-conditioned learning framework that jointly models nanoparticle physicochemical properties and protein sequence representations. Using frozen ESM-2 embeddings and a joint interaction transformer, NanoPCT learns transferable representations of nano-bio interaction patterns across hundreds of proteins and maintains robust performance as protein diversity increases. The learned protein representation further enables zero-shot prediction for previously unseen proteins and biologically distinct protein groups through classifier reconstruction in embedding space. Beyond prediction, NanoPCT supports large-scale in silico inverse design and reveals consistent adsorption preferences between observed and unseen protein populations, suggesting that it captures transferable interaction patterns rather than protein-specific memorization. NanoPCT provides a unified framework for protein corona prediction, zero-shot generalization, and rational nanomaterial design.

papers.title: AI-guided discovery for low-resource peptide engineering using evolutionary scale modeling
papers.abstract: Data scarcity is a major bottleneck in artificial intelligence (AI)-guided peptide engineering, where experimental training sets often contain only tens to a few hundred sequences, and it is difficult to judge in advance whether a protein language model (PLM) will effectively guide iterative discovery before committing to wet-lab work. Here we present SCARSE, a machine learning framework that couples ESM2 protein language model embeddings with Gaussian process regression. Benchmarked across 24 diverse peptide and small-protein datasets spanning substitution and indel variants, antimicrobial peptides, and hemolytic peptides, SCARSE significantly outperformed hand-engineered descriptor baselines on substitution and indel tasks in low-data regimes (20-500 training samples) and performed comparably on short non-mutant peptides. In active learning simulations it consistently prioritized high-performing candidates, discovering up to 7-fold more top-tier peptides than random sampling. Cross-validation (CV) R2 correlated strongly with final active learning performance (Pearson r = 0.80-0.84), and evaluating on as few as 50 labeled peptides reduced CV R2 variance enough for it to serve as a practical, data-efficient criterion for assessing model suitability before iterative screening. SCARSE thus provides an early diagnostic indicator for active learning success and is freely available as an open-source Python package (pip) and through an interactive Hugging Face Spaces web interface.

papers.title: Drug screen and machine learning predict neuroprotective agents in a preclinical human model of childhood dementia.
papers.abstract: Childhood dementias are a group of paediatric neurodegenerative disorders characterised by neurocognitive decline, and in many cases underpinned by pathophysiological mechanisms similar to adult-onset dementias. In this study, we use patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from children with one of the most prevalent childhood dementias, Mucopolysaccharidosis Type IIIA (MPS IIIA), also known as Sanfilippo syndrome. The derived cortical cultures exhibit lysosomal dysfunction, heparan sulfate accumulation, progressive neurodegeneration and astrocytic reactivity, recapitulating prototypical in-vivo phenotypes. Using a multimodal drug screening platform that integrates machine learning, high-content confocal imaging, single-nuclei transcriptomics and electrophysiology, we identify at least nine repurposed compounds that significantly mitigate these adverse effects within two weeks of treatment in vitro, demonstrating potential for rapid clinical translation. This human preclinical model for MPS IIIA, coupled with a robust multimodal therapeutic interrogation platform, serves as an exemplar for advancing drug discovery for childhood dementias and the broader neurodegenerative disease spectrum.

papers.title: CellChain: Benchmarking Cross-Scale Evidence Use for Perturbation Reasoning
papers.abstract: Recent advances in foundation models and large-scale cellular perturbation datasets have driven growing interest in using LLMs to predict and reason about cellular responses. Biological reasoning in this setting involves relating molecular mechanisms, cellular responses, and functional outcomes across scales. Evaluating foundation models therefore requires assessing not only whether their predictions are correct, but also how those predictions depend on the biological evidence provided. We introduce CellChain, an experimentally grounded benchmark comprising 590 biological cases and 2,360 matched evidence-condition instances across gene-dependency prediction, cytokine-axis identification, and drug-sensitivity ranking. CellChain links perturbation experiments and external biological resources through a provenance-aware evidence graph spanning molecular, pathway, transcriptional, and phenotypic information. Task-specific conditions vary evidence coverage, composition, or assignment while preserving questions, candidate answers, reference targets, and scoring rules. Across 18 foundation models, the highest accuracies under prespecified target-evidence conditions are 57.5%, 75.5%, and 70.8%, respectively, and broader evidence coverage does not consistently improve accuracy. On the drug-sensitivity benchmark cohort, matched reference histories outperform swapped histories by an average of 13.0 percentage points in cluster-weighted accuracy. Decision-transition analysis separates corrections, newly introduced errors, and wrong-answer switches, revealing substantial answer changes hidden by small net accuracy differences. CellChain provides controlled comparisons for attributing changes in model predictions to prespecified expansions of biological context, including changes in evidence coverage, composition, and biological assignment.

papers.title: Comparative analysis of mitochondrial proteomes across the tree of life.
papers.abstract: Mitochondria arose from the endosymbiosis of a bacterium with an archaea-related host cell about 2 billion years ago. To understand their origins and evolution, we compared experimentally defined mitoproteomes from the MitoCarta Tree of Life project. Across eight organisms, we identified 8,619 distinct mitochondrial proteins within 3,199 families, of which 43% lack Pfam domains. We report 33 protein families conserved in eukaryotic pathogens yet absent in humans, representing promising candidate targets for protozoan infectious diseases. Leveraging our experimentally defined mitoproteomes, we retrained a classifier based on a protein language model to predict mitoproteomes of ∼200 eukaryotes. From this expanded set, we detail the evolutionary trajectories of mitochondria, ranging from clade-specific gene family expansions to extreme mitoproteome reductions seemingly en route to complete organelle loss. Finally, we reconstruct the last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA) mitoproteome, revealing that LECA possessed a complex mitochondrion capable of both aerobic and anaerobic metabolism.

papers.title: Generative AI designs functional thiolation domains for reprogramming non-ribosomal peptide synthetases.
papers.abstract: Large language models and generative protein design promise to accelerate biotechnology, but it remains unclear whether they can engineer dynamic megasynth(et)ases whose activity depends on transient, context-specific domain interfaces. Non-ribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) exemplify this challenge and produce many clinically used therapeutics. Here we integrate pretrained generative models (ESM3, ProteinMPNN and EvoDiff) with design-build-test-learn cycles and data-guided prioritization to generate 76 de novo thiolation (T) domains. We build and test 578 recombinant NRPS variants in vivo spanning minimal, full-length, and hybrid assembly lines. AI-designed T-domains support product formation across architectures, enable catalytically active hybrids at recombined junctions, and increase yields by up to ~3-fold relative to NRPSs carrying the native T-domain. A representative design shows improved soluble expression, refolding, and a 12 °C higher melting temperature, while molecular dynamics simulations indicate preserved global stability but reshaped, state-dependent interdomain contact networks. Together, these results establish generative design as an effective route to context-conditioned engineering and reprogramming of biosynthetic assembly lines.

papers.title: GENA-LM: a family of open-source foundational DNA language models for long sequences
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in genomics, propelled by artificial intelligence, have unlocked unprecedented capabilities in interpreting genomic sequences, mitigating the need for exhaustive experimental analysis of complex, intertwined molecular processes inherent in DNA function. A significant challenge, however, resides in accurately decoding genomic sequences, which inherently involves comprehending rich contextual information dispersed across thousands of nucleotides. To address this need, we introduce GENA language model (GENA-LM), a suite of transformer-based foundational DNA language models capable of handling input lengths up to 36 000 base pairs. Notably, integrating the newly developed recurrent memory mechanism allows these models to process even larger DNA segments. We provide pre-trained versions of GENA-LM, including multispecies and taxon-specific models, demonstrating their capability for fine-tuning and addressing a spectrum of complex biological tasks with modest computational demands. While language models have already achieved significant breakthroughs in protein biology, GENA-LM showcases a similarly promising potential for reshaping the landscape of genomics and multi-omics data analysis. All models are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/AIRI-Institute/GENA_LM) and on HuggingFace (https://huggingface.co/AIRI-Institute). In addition, we provide a web service (https://dnalm.airi.net/) allowing user-friendly DNA annotation with GENA-LM models.

papers.title: Generating protein hydrogels with customizable stress relaxation behavior via deep learning-driven entanglement design.
papers.abstract: Protein hydrogels are promising artificial extracellular matrices (ECMs) for 3D stem cell and organoid culture due to their favorable stress relaxation behavior (a decrease in stress in response to strain). Inter-chain entangled motifs, in which different protein chains are interlaced, represent a powerful strategy to synthesize such hydrogels. However, designing these motifs with tailored properties such as binding energy remains a major challenge due to the difficulty of simultaneously controlling these properties while ensuring entanglement. Here, we introduce TangleDiff, a deep learning framework for the de novo design of homodimeric entangled proteins with programmable features. TangleDiff generates diverse foldable entangled sequences with an in-silico success rate exceeding 70%, markedly outperforming current models (~1%). By conditioning TangleDiff on inter-chain binding energy, we generate novel protein dimers whose binding energies closely match the specified ranges, with approximately 70% of successful designs conforming to expected values. We experimentally validate TangleDiff by designing nine homodimers targeting various binding energies; seven successfully form hydrogels, with stress relaxation dynamics correlated with specified binding energies. This work establishes a general strategy for entangled protein design, opening avenues for entanglement-based biomaterial innovation.

papers.title: DeepTTA: a transformer-based model for predicting cancer drug response
papers.abstract: Identifying new lead molecules to treat cancer requires more than a decade of dedicated effort. Before selected drug candidates are used in the clinic, their anti-cancer activity is generally validated by in vitro cellular experiments. Therefore, accurate prediction of cancer drug response is a critical and challenging task for anti-cancer drugs design and precision medicine. With the development of pharmacogenomics, the combination of efficient drug feature extraction methods and omics data has made it possible to use computational models to assist in drug response prediction. In this study, we propose DeepTTA, a novel end-to-end deep learning model that utilizes transformer for drug representation learning and a multilayer neural network for transcriptomic data prediction of the anti-cancer drug responses. Specifically, DeepTTA uses transcriptomic gene expression data and chemical substructures of drugs for drug response prediction. Compared to existing methods, DeepTTA achieved higher performance in terms of root mean square error, Pearson correlation coefficient and Spearman's rank correlation coefficient on multiple test sets. Moreover, we discovered that anti-cancer drugs bortezomib and dactinomycin provide a potential therapeutic option with multiple clinical indications. With its excellent performance, DeepTTA is expected to be an effective method in cancer drug design.

papers.title: Interpretable machine learning enables de novo mapping of cell type-specific RNA splicing regulation from scRNA-seq data.
papers.abstract: Context-dependent regulation of alternative splicing, largely mediated by RNA-binding proteins, is a key post-transcriptional mechanism shaping diverse biological processes. Experimental approaches for probing splicing regulation, such as crosslinking-immunoprecipitation assays and RNA-binding protein perturbations, suffer from low throughput, poor physiological relevance, and bulk resolution that overlooks cellular heterogeneity. Here, we present CASREL, a machine learning framework that reconstructs candidate regulatory circuitry between RNA-binding proteins and alternative splicing directly from single-cell RNA sequencing data without reliance on prior protein-RNA binding annotations. CASREL integrates ensemble learning with model interpretation based on Shapley additive explanations to infer associations between RNA-binding proteins and alternative splicing, leveraging distinctive features of single-cell splicing profiles, including polarized isoform usage, minimal averaging of regulatory programs, and resilience to expression noise. Applications across diverse tissues and cell types demonstrate its robustness, accuracy, and biological relevance, supporting CASREL as an effective method for de novo mapping of putative cell-specific RNA splicing regulation in physiological contexts.

papers.title: A moving target: non-stationary selection governs unsupervised prediction of viral fitness
papers.abstract: Anticipating how mutations change viral fitness is central to genomic surveillance and vaccine design. However, the phenotypic data behind the most accurate supervised variant-effect predictors is unavailable for most emerging pathogens. It is therefore unclear how a label-free, unsupervised approach would perform using only sequences, their evolutionary history, and their protein structure. To address this outstanding question, we assemble a modular, fully unsupervised pipeline that estimates key interpretable terms: intrinsic replicative fitness, antigenic escape, and realized growth. Each term is produced by more than one estimator, so that the fitness predictor becomes a testable model choice. Benchmarking the intrinsic term on 21 viral deep-mutational-scanning assays from ProteinGym, we find that a 650-million-parameter single-sequence protein language model (PLM) is a weak predictor of viral fitness, whereas a simple site-independent alignment model more than doubles performance, with the largest gains obtained for the antigenic surface proteins not included in the training of the PLM. On the other hand, PMLs based on protein alignment (MSA Transformer, Tranception) regain the accuracy lost with the single-sequence PML, but do not significantly exceed the simple alignment. Therefore, the most important feature to predict viral fitness is the protein alignment, not model scale or architecture. Our central result is evolutionary: using dated sequences of SARS-CoV-2 spike and influenza H3N2 hemagglutinin, we find that the epoch of the alignment is itself a virus-specific determinant of accuracy. This demonstrates that selection is a non-stationary process, in a manner that is itself virus-specific. A phylogenetic mutation-selection estimator of fitness does not match the far simpler and less computationally expensive alignment model. Altogether, this work shows that unsupervised viral fitness prediction is as much an evolutionary problem as a modeling one.

papers.title: Multi-omics atlas of chronic exercise.
papers.abstract: Exercise reduces all-cause mortality, yet its molecular effects across organs, sexes, and circadian phases remain incompletely understood. We subjected mice to 8 weeks of voluntary wheel running and collected 22 tissues and plasma during active and inactive phases for bulk RNA sequencing, metabolomics, proteomics, and single-nucleus RNA and methylation sequencing. Exercise induced canonical fiber-type switching and widespread, tissue-specific remodeling, with the largest transcriptomic changes in skeletal muscle. Except for the hypothalamus, kidney, and lung, most tissues changed more during the active phase. Females showed broader transcriptional responses, with distinct downregulation. Pairing single-nucleus methylomes with transcriptomes resolved the cell types driving exercise-induced epigenetic remodeling-changes undetectable by bulk studies. These included coordinated gene-body demethylation and transcription that tracked with fiber-type switching in specific myonuclei. Cell-type-resolved methylation, including partially methylated domains characterized in muscle, revealed a strong, sex-biased epigenetic response to training. Machine learning identified conserved exercise signatures across mammalian species.

papers.title: Integrate multi-omics data with biological interaction networks using Multi-view Factorization AutoEncoder (MAE)
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Comprehensive molecular profiling of various cancers and other diseases has generated vast amounts of multi-omics data. Each type of -omics data corresponds to one feature space, such as gene expression, miRNA expression, DNA methylation, etc. Integrating multi-omics data can link different layers of molecular feature spaces and is crucial to elucidate molecular pathways underlying various diseases. Machine learning approaches to mining multi-omics data hold great promises in uncovering intricate relationships among molecular features. However, due to the "big p, small n" problem (i.e., small sample sizes with high-dimensional features), training a large-scale generalizable deep learning model with multi-omics data alone is very challenging. RESULTS: We developed a method called Multi-view Factorization AutoEncoder (MAE) with network constraints that can seamlessly integrate multi-omics data and domain knowledge such as molecular interaction networks. Our method learns feature and patient embeddings simultaneously with deep representation learning. Both feature representations and patient representations are subject to certain constraints specified as regularization terms in the training objective. By incorporating domain knowledge into the training objective, we implicitly introduced a good inductive bias into the machine learning model, which helps improve model generalizability. We performed extensive experiments on the TCGA datasets and demonstrated the power of integrating multi-omics data and biological interaction networks using our proposed method for predicting target clinical variables. CONCLUSIONS: To alleviate the overfitting problem in deep learning on multi-omics data with the "big p, small n" problem, it is helpful to incorporate biological domain knowledge into the model as inductive biases. It is very promising to design machine learning models that facilitate the seamless integration of large-scale multi-omics data and biomedical domain knowledge for uncovering intricate relationships among molecular features and clinical features.

papers.title: How Much Can AI Virtual Cells Gain from Unified Perturbational Modeling?
papers.abstract: Predicting how individual cells respond to perturbations is a central task in artificial intelligence virtual cell (AIVC) modeling. However, integrating perturbation datasets is challenging because they differ in measured gene sets, perturbation types and cellular contexts. Existing AIVC predictors are typically developed for specific settings, limiting their applicability across heterogeneous datasets. Here, we investigate the extent to which AIVC predictors can benefit from unified perturbational modeling (UPM), a novel paradigm designed to integrate heterogeneous Perturb-seq datasets into a single predictive model. To this end, we introduce three unification modules into a variational autoencoder (VAE)-based AIVC predictor to address these sources of heterogeneity: gene-channel alignment, shared perturbation encoding, and joint embedding of gene expression and identity. We systematically evaluate and validate the individual contributions of these modules. Building on UPM, we assemble a dataset of 110 million cells spanning over 22,000 genes, four perturbation types and 76 cellular contexts, and use 89.7 million cells from 71 contexts to train a unified AIVC predictor with more than one billion parameters. Across genetic perturbation benchmarks, UPM achieves the highest PES and gene-wise response correlation among the evaluated models. It also improves all four evaluation metrics over State on the five held-out Tahoe-100M cell lines and over Stack on the cytokine benchmark. UPM also improves combinatorial perturbation prediction relative to specialized predictors. In the HSC application, our model achieves a 40.0% improvement in accuracy on a downstream task involving the recapitulation of effects induced by the knockdown of hepatic stellate cell (HSC)-related targets. Our implementation is openly available at https://github.com/youlab2025/UPM.

papers.title: Creator 1.0: Phylogeny-Guided Stagewise Pretraining for Plant Genome Foundation Models across 1,000 Species
papers.abstract: Genomic language models have advanced DNA sequence analysis, but their applicability to plant-specific tasks and representation changes during pretraining remain poorly characterized. Here, we present Creator 1.0, a 2-billion-parameter parameter plant genome foundation model pretrained on 1,000 plant genomes using phylogeny-guided stagewise pretraining (PGSP). Training comprised 83 consecutive stages and produced 52 cumulative checkpoints associated with distinct plant orders. On GENEB, the stage 83 checkpoint ranked first among 46 models across 10 plant-related tasks, with a mean Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.565, and fourth across all 100 tasks. Evaluation of 52 checkpoints on six plant lncRNA tasks identified different optimal stages under full-data, 10-shot and 1-shot settings, corresponding to stages 71, 72 and 29, respectively. Checkpoint performance varied across tasks, without consistent advantages for corresponding plant orders. These findings demonstrate the competitive performance of Creator 1.0 and highlight the potential of PGSP to provide task-adaptable checkpoints for plant genomic applications.

papers.title: Predicting clonal mutations from tumour spatial transcriptomics data using a graph convolutional neural network
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) has revolutionized our understanding of tumour biology but inherently lacks information on the upstream somatic driver mutations. We developed a spatially-aware graph convolutional neural network approach (SPOT-Mut) that infers mutated (sub)clones directly from ST data. SPOT-Mut was trained on virtual ST slides with clones simulated from a large collection of existing RNA and matched DNA sequencing data. SPOT-Mut was first evaluated for predicting mutations in TP53, the most frequently mutated gene in human cancer. Precision and recall values exceeded 95% in most analysed cancer types and the model was validated on ST and matched DNA sequencing data from serial slices obtained from cutaneous SCC samples. SPOT-Mut was then trained on 62 frequently mutated driver genes, resulting in highly performing somatic mutation prediction models for 40 driver genes, including KRAS, KEAP1, CTNNB1 and APC. With the increasing availability of ST data and upcoming atlases, SPOT-Mut potentiates the localization of (sub)clonal alterations in TP53 and other common driver mutations.

papers.title: Structure, Not Sequence: Tracking and Validating Folding Mechanisms in ESMFold's Trunk with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.abstract: Structure predictors like ESMFold fold proteins using neural network computation and have transformed structural biology. However, the driving mechanism from amino-acid (AA) sequence to 3D structure is insufficiently understood, and biological meaning remains locked in the dense network. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promising results in obtaining interpretable concept features over an overcomplete basis of intermediate protein sequence-model representations. Yet folding models, which predict physical shape from AA sequence semantics, have no such account. We hypothesize that the features carrying the folding computation evolve in the 3D structural regression process. In this paper, we interpret the folding trunk in three steps. First, a pilot analysis on the representation distribution across modules and recycles locates distinct spatial computation in the trunk. Second, the dictionaries expose a division of labor: the single representation carries inherited semantics, and the pair representation computes the pairwise geometry. Third, we interpret the dictionary at scale with a reasoning language model, trace how the concepts compose across blocks by gradient-based attribution, and follow the interpreted code to the model's folding output, verifying where the computation aligns with, or departs from, known biochemistry. Together, the sparse dictionaries we train capture the relational geometry the trunk computes beyond the sequence model, and their concept activations forecast the model's own fold quality, turning the black-box folding trunk into a sparse, interpretable, and scientifically verifiable circuit.

papers.title: Stronger artificial intelligence breakthroughs hasten their own exhaustion
papers.abstract: Progress in artificial intelligence is widely assumed to scale with effort: more researchers, papers and investment should accelerate discovery. Theories of technological growth instead locate the difficulty of discovery in the space of ideas. Here we show that neither scale nor space is enough: breakthroughs depend on diverse attention, which collective concentration can deplete. Across 36 years of computer science, we analyze 7.2 million papers, 73,089 peer reviews and 3.7 million researchers and their topic shifts. The field expanded while its attention narrowed sharply after the Transformer. Over half of topic-shifting researchers moved into AI, especially mid-career ones, and reviewer confidence fell by a full point on a 5-point scale. Each successive breakthrough, from AlexNet to large language models, raised the field's carrying capacity for ideas but was followed by steeper exhaustion of those ideas. Bigger breakthroughs capture attention more completely, depleting the diversity their successors may draw upon. Structural biology shows the same cycle after cryo-EM and AlphaFold. Simulations show how well-intentioned and widely used policies such as reciprocal reviewing empower prolific authors and further narrow what the field accepts. We call for institutions that protect diverse attention in artificial intelligence rather than reward concentration on the winning paradigm.

papers.title: Protein novelty, sequence similarity, and negative sampling controls reveal benchmark specific discrimination in protein protein interactionprediction
papers.abstract: Protein protein interaction (PPI) predictors are often evaluated with random pair splits that permit proteins to recur across training and test sets, while constructed negative pairs can introduce a separate source of benchmark-specific signal. We reassessed the Guo yeast benchmark using a matched protein novelty curve, independently generated MMseqs2 sequence cluster controlled R3 variants, topology only controls, degree- and length matched putative negatives, handcrafted and frozen protein language model representations, multiple model configurations, seed analyses, and connected component aware inference. In the matched R1[->]R2[->]R3 comparison, AAC+CTD-MLP ROC-AUC declined from 0.697 for seen-seen pairs to 0.626 for one-unseen pairs and 0.587 for both-unseen pairs. Across independently regenerated cluster-disjoint R3 variants at 50%, 40%, 30%, and 20% MMseqs2 clustering thresholds, performance showed no consistent monotonic trend. Guo original-negative endpoints had lower positive-network degree than positive endpoints (mean 3.34 versus 6.72), and a degree-only logistic model reached ROC-AUC 0.962 on the original negatives but 0.502 on degree-matched negatives. We used degree-matched negatives consistently for R3 training and testing; six sequence based model configurations yielded ROC-AUC 0.493- 0.547; none showed corrected connected-component-aware evidence of above-chance discrimination. A PIPR multispecies analysis reproduced degree-associated label separation but also exposed cross-species pairing as an additional pooled cue. These results show that protein novelty, operational sequence cluster separation, and negative-set topology are distinct dimensions of PPI benchmark evaluation. The Guo result is benchmark-specific and should not be generalized to sequence-based PPI prediction or protein language models overall. The dataset and source code for the experiments are publicly available at https://github.com/morufwork/guoAudit.git.

papers.title: Transcriptomic rejuvenation during intestinal and liver regeneration in mice
papers.abstract: Aging and regeneration are fundamental biological processes, but the relationship between them is poorly understood. During intestinal regeneration, adult epithelial cells reactivate developmental programs that support repair. To investigate if this plasticity alters tissue biological age, we developed and validated intestinal tissue and epithelium-specific transcriptomic aging clocks. Across various regeneration models, epithelial states were predicted by these clocks to be younger than controls. Their expression changes were also negatively associated with intestinal stem-cell and progenitor aging signatures. The resulting younger state was characterized by YAP-associated regeneration and reduced mature enterocyte identity. In a separate irradiation model, the predicted epithelial age first increased, then fell at the peak of regeneration and later increased again during recovery. In a chemotherapy-induced injury model, epithelium in both young and old animals also reversibly transitioned through this younger state, returning to its preinjury state during recovery, although regenerative and fetal-like gene expression differed with host age. Further spatial transcriptomic analyses linked lower epithelial age with regeneration in selected injured and tumor-associated regions. In addition, liver regeneration after partial hepatectomy in old animals was also accompanied by decreased transcriptomic age, which persisted to the last sampled time point, and by pathway changes negatively associated with aging signatures. Overall, these findings suggest that mammalian regeneration is associated with a transient reduction in transcriptomic age, whose timing and persistence depend on tissue and the course of repair.

papers.title: Benchmarking LLM-based Information Extraction Tools for Medical Documents
papers.abstract: Background: Medical documents are a crucial resource for medical research around the world. While troves of valuable health data exist, they are largely computationally inaccessible as hard copies of unstructured text. Moreover, the persistent prevalence of fax machines in medical settings contributes to further degradation of document quality. Manual data extraction from these documents is time-consuming and resource intensive. However, large language models (LLMs) have recently shown great promise for automated digitization and information extraction (IE), greatly improving upon previous technologies in terms of accuracy. Objective: Here we aim to survey the landscape of LLM-based IE tools with respect to their applicability to biomedical documents and to systematically benchmark them on synthetic documents with paired reference extractions. We put special focus on locally executable tools and models that suit privacy- and resource-constrained settings. Methods: We reviewed LLM-based IE tools from the literature and assessed them with respect to their suitability for use in biomedical research. We found only one of these tools (NuExtract2) to satisfy our selection criteria and compared it to LLM foundation models prompted to perform extractions. We created 200 mock molecular test reports with paired reference data using a bespoke procedural generation approach and evaluated the tools' performance across different prompting strategies, input modalities, and document qualities. Results: We found model performance to be very sensitive to input modalities and quality. The best overall performance was observed for the proprietary GPT 4.1-mini, with an F1 score of 79.2% averaged across quality levels and modalities. The best performing open-weights model was Mistral-small 3.1 with an average F1 score of 76.2%. The NuExtract2 model was the only one able to run on regular laptop computers, but did not perform well. Surprisingly, we found the choice of one-shot over zero-shot prompts to only have a small effect size on extraction performance in most cases. Conclusions: LLMs place the automatic processing of highly complex medical documents in resource-constrained and privacy-sensitive settings within reach, but still require human oversight. Availability: Source code and data are available on GitHub and on Zenodo, respectively.

papers.title: Current gaps in downstream applications of fMRI foundation models: lessons learned from BrainLM & BrainHarmonix on Prevent-AD
papers.abstract: Foundation models have driven major advancements in the language and vision domains, as seen in the popularity of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools, and a growing number of studies are bringing the approach to human brain imaging. Whether these models are ready for independent researchers to use on clinical datasets has yet to be examined. We evaluated two recent fMRI foundation models, BrainLM and BrainHarmonix, on PreventAD, a dataset on adults with a family history of Alzheimer's disease. We compared features from frozen and fine-tuned models against two baselines: functional connectivity and a dummy classifier that always predicts the most common class. The sample includes 343 subjects who passed quality control, with a subset of 218 who had amyloid PET imaging. We tested four prediction targets: sex, age, progression to mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and {beta}-amyloid burden. Both models required substantial changes to the released code. BrainLM's own data preparation workflow did not produce stable fine-tuning, which we achieved only after switching to a standard workflow implemented with the library Nilearn. BrainHarmonix's documentation did not specify how to normalize new data, so we resolved this by testing different alternatives. For sex, functional connectivity outperformed all foundation model features. For age group, the best foundation model feature, taken from BrainHarmonix's structural (T1-weighted) encoder, slightly exceeded functional connectivity, but the difference was not significant. For MCI and {beta}-amyloid, no feature exceeded the dummy classifier in accuracy, and the area under the curve (AUC) stayed near chance for all features. For both clinical targets, the most precise feature came from fine-tuned BrainLM, meaning a larger share of its positive predictions were correct than for functional connectivity, but neither difference reached statistical significance. These results suggested that the strong transfer to new tasks seen in large language models cannot yet be assumed for fMRI foundation models, and that both models required code adaptation that would preclude their streamlined adoption by independent groups. We recommend that future studies provide standardized data workflows and always report functional connectivity and dummy classifier baselines. For clinical targets with strong class imbalance, studies should report several metrics, including precision.

papers.title: Genomic foundation models do not yet boost common variant discovery beyond standard functional annotations
papers.abstract: Genomic foundation models (GFMs) use large-scale AI to model genetic sequences and their influence on molecular phenotypes. While GFMs have shown promise in rare variant analysis, their utility for common variant discovery remains untested. Using the surrogate functional false discovery rate framework for functionally informed GWAS discovery, we compared standard functional annotations (baselineLD) with annotations derived from three leading GFMs: the sequence-to-function models AlphaGenome and Borzoi, and the genomic language model GPN-Star. Across 27 UK Biobank traits, GPN-Star decreased locus discovery relative to a standard GWAS, whereas AlphaGenome and Borzoi increased discovery but by less than baselineLD (medians 1.8%, 3.8%, and 5.1%). When we combined the GFM and baselineLD annotations, there was no increase over baselineLD alone (median changes -0.1% to 0.2%), suggesting that AlphaGenome and Borzoi mostly capture information already in baselineLD. Thus, GFMs may require larger corpora or trait-specific feature engineering to improve discovery beyond standard functional annotations.

papers.title: Characterization of hypothetical proteins reveals function modules and virulence factors in Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
papers.abstract: Hypothetical proteins (HPs), known as biological dark matter, are genetic sequences of which the biological functions and regulatory processes remain largely unclear. In Pseudomonas aeruginosa, HPs account for 36.4% of all coding genes, representing a significant gap in understanding their functions and contribution to the virulence network. To address these challenges, we present a deletion repertoire comprising 938 strains targeting 1165 HPs in P. aeruginosa. Starting with transcriptome-wide analysis, we inferred putative functional predictions for HP mutants through systematic profiling of differential expression and candidate transcriptional pathways. We integrated our expression profiles with public datasets (5707 genes × 2312 conditions). This allowed us to distinguish constitutively expressed genes from variable genes. Using independent component analysis (ICA), we identified 56 independent regulatory Modules, providing a comprehensive transcriptional-association framework. These contributed to the discovery and experimental validation of 20 virulence-related hypothetical proteins (VRHPs) and 3 antibiotic resistance-related hypothetical proteins (ARHPs). Evolutionary analysis across bacterial taxa provided additional insights into HP sequence conservation and evolutionary dynamics. In summary, our study presents a large-scale HP mutant library combined with integrated transcriptomic and machine learning approaches, establishing both a valuable resource and a systematic strategy for predicting and prioritizing candidate functions of HPs across bacterial species.

papers.title: Synergy-Aware Residual Flow Matching for Single-Cell Perturbation Prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting single-cell responses to genetic and chemical perturbations is important for understanding regulatory mechanisms and prioritizing therapeutic interventions. Existing methods have made progress by modeling perturbation-conditioned expression shifts with neural networks, graph priors, foundation-model representations, or distributional generative models. However, combinatorial perturbation prediction remains challenging because much of the response can be explained by additive single-perturbation effects, while the biologically informative signal often lies in a smaller non-additive residual induced by perturbation interactions. Directly generating the full post-perturbation expression profile may therefore allocate substantial capacity to the dominant additive component and underemphasize synergy-specific structure. To address this issue, we propose \textbf{SynGeneFlow}, a synergy-aware flow matching framework that anchors the source distribution at an additive prior and learns a residual flow toward the true perturbed state. SynGeneFlow further incorporates perturbation-conditioned gene interaction modeling, where a static gene-gene mask provides biological structure and a perturbation-dependent deformation bias dynamically modulates gene-gene coupling. To preserve population-level response structure, we align both endpoint distributions and biological residual distributions with MMD-based regularization. We evaluate SynGeneFlow on genetic and drug perturbation benchmarks under observed-single, held-out, and cross-modality settings. The results demonstrate that residualizing flow matching around additive perturbation effects provides a biologically grounded and robust framework for single-cell perturbation response prediction.

papers.title: ProtGPT2 is a deep unsupervised language model for protein design
papers.abstract: Abstract Protein design aims to build new proteins from scratch thereby holding the potential to tackle many environmental and biomedical problems. Recent progress in the field of natural language processing (NLP) has enabled the implementation of ever-growing language models capable of understanding and generating text with human-like capabilities. Given the many similarities between human languages and protein sequences, the use of NLP models offers itself for predictive tasks in protein research. Motivated by the evident success of generative Transformer-based language models such as the GPT-x series, we developed ProtGPT2, a language model trained on protein space that generates de novo protein sequences that follow the principles of natural ones. In particular, the generated proteins display amino acid propensities which resemble natural proteins. Disorder and secondary structure prediction indicate that 88% of ProtGPT2-generated proteins are globular, in line with natural sequences.
