papers.abstract: Lysosome membrane permeabilization (LMP) is an emerging signature of neurodegenerative diseases, yet the mechanisms that enable an effective repair are largely undefined, particularly in neurons. Here, we reveal sorting nexin (SNX) proteins SNX13 and SNX14 maintain lysosome membrane lipid composition to support efficient LMP repair and neuronal survival. We identify loss of function mutations in SNX13 in children manifesting a previously unrecognized cerebellar neurodegenerative disorder. Consistently, Snx13 ablation in mice causes cerebellar Purkinje cell death and signatures of ataxia-like motor deficits. We show loss of SNX13 or its ataxia-linked paralog SNX14 perturbs lysosome morphology, positioning, and acidity and causes increased susceptibility to lysosome damage. Using lysosome immunoprecipitation and proteomics, we comprehensively map lysosome proteome remodeling during membrane damage and repair, finding that SNX13 or SNX14 deficiency blunts recruitment of repair machinery, including ESCRTs and PITT pathway proteins, to damaged lysosomes. Mechanistically, we determine SNX13 and SNX14 support lysosome integrity through interorganelle lipid crosstalk. We define SNX13 and SNX14 as lipid binding proteins that localize to ER-lysosome junctions, where they support lysosomal phosphoinositide levels in response to membrane damage. In line with this, loss of SNX13 or SNX14 impairs lysosome PtdIns4P signaling. Altogether, our work reveals a conserved mechanism of interorganelle lipid crosstalk by SNX13/14 family proteins that safeguards lysosome membranes, maintaining them competent for repair, and is defective in cerebellar neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Predicting HPV/p16 Status and Molecular Subtypes from Histopathology Slides using Deep Learning in Vulvar Squamous Cell Carcinoma
papers.abstract: Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma (VSCC) comprises three prognostically distinct molecular subtypes: human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated, HPV-independent/p53-wildtype, and HPV-independent/p53-abnormal. Classification requires p16/p53 immunohistochemistry, which consumes tissue and is often incomplete in retrospective cohorts. We investigated whether deep learning could predict HPV/p16 status and molecular subtypes directly from routine hematoxylin and eosin-stained whole-slide images. Using features extracted with H-optimus-1, we developed two attention-based multiple-instance learning models: HERA, predicting HPV/p16 status, and HERMES, predicting the three molecular subtypes. Models were developed on 644 patients from three Dutch VSCC cohorts and tested on 286 patients from two independent cohorts. In independent testing, HERA achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.84 (95% CI 0.75-0.91), with specificity 0.93, negative predictive value 0.94, and sensitivity 0.68. HERA-predicted groups reproduced the prognostic separation of HPV testing (log-rank p<0.001). HERMES achieved a macro-average AUC of 0.70 (0.66-0.75), with good discrimination for HPV-associated (0.80) but limited separation of HPV-independent/p53-abnormal (AUC 0.68) and HPV-independent/p53-wildtype (AUC 0.63). HERMES-predicted classes reproduced the prognostic hierarchy, with 5-year recurrence rates of 14.0% (HPV-associated), 31.1% (HPV-independent/p53-wildtype) and 43.3% (HPV-independent/p53-abnormal) (p=0.0051). Highly attended tiles showed basaloid cells and koilocytotic-like atypia in HPV-associated tumors, keratinizing nests with desmoplastic stroma in HPV-independent/p53-abnormal tumors, and well-differentiated keratinocytes with spongiosis in HPV-independent/p53-wildtype tumors. HERA could assign HPV/p16 status to large retrospective VSCC cohorts lacking ancillary testing, without consuming tissue, enabling HPV-stratified outcome analyses. Before such use, external validation of its discrimination and calibration across scanners and populations is required. HERMES suggests that molecular subtype information is encoded in hematoxylin and eosin-stained slides, but requires improved distinction between the HPV-independent subtypes.

papers.title: The Effectiveness and Durability of Pretraining Data Filtering in Protein Language Models
papers.abstract: Pretraining filtering is one of the most common safeguards for open-weight language models. Here we study its effectiveness, durability and scalability using the ESM-2 family of protein language models. We find that filtering viral proteins from the pretraining data meaningfully degrades masked language modelling, mutation effect prediction and long-range contact prediction on viral proteins, while largely preserving performance on non-viral proteins. These effects are concentrated among proteins from human-infecting viruses, and grow as we scale models from 8M to 3B parameters. As models increase in size, we find that stringent filtering becomes more effective. However, fine-tuning on sequences from the removed viral families restores the lost performance. Although the cost to recover performance increases with model scale, even for the largest models it costs about 80 USD of H100 time. This work establishes pretraining filtering as moderately effective at selectively degrading performance on viral proteins, but not durable against fine-tuning with modest computational resources and access to relevant data.

papers.title: PRISM: Prior Relational Information for Self-supervised Modeling to Enhance Solubility OOD Generalization
papers.abstract: Solubility depends on intermolecular interactions between solutes and solvents, and is central to drug discovery, chemical and materials process engineering. Its prediction requires out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization to unseen solutes, solvents, and solvent mixtures, where supervised methods suffer from data scarcity, and existing self-supervised methods do not explicitly learn chemically meaningful relations. Learning chemically meaningful relational information without labels can alleviate data scarcity and improve OOD generalization, but remains challenging. We introduce Prior Relational Information for Self-supervised Modeling (PRISM) and apply it to solubility OOD generalization. PRISM is a label-free pretraining framework that converts expert-defined chemical priors into relational teachers. For solubility prediction, it trains four encoders to preserve the population-level relational information from priors capturing hydrophobic, electrostatic, polarizability, and substructural effects, using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence to match distance-based neighborhood distributions during pretraining. Across scaffold, solute, and solvent OOD settings, PRISM matches or surpasses supervised and self-supervised baselines. Under mixed-solvent OOD, freezing the four PRISM encoders and training a lightweight fusion-and-composition head outperforms strong baselines and substantially reduces run-to-run variation. Ablations and control studies confirm that gains stem from chemically meaningful relational structures baked into the encoders by PRISM. We expect this strategy of turning relational priors into self-supervision signals to extend beyond solubility prediction to domains where chemically or biologically meaningful relational priors are available.

papers.title: Transformer for one stop interpretable cell type annotation
papers.abstract: Consistent annotation transfer from reference dataset to query dataset is fundamental to the development and reproducibility of single-cell research. Compared with traditional annotation methods, deep learning based methods are faster and more automated. A series of useful single cell analysis tools based on autoencoder architecture have been developed but these struggle to strike a balance between depth and interpretability. Here, we present TOSICA, a multi-head self-attention deep learning model based on Transformer that enables interpretable cell type annotation using biologically understandable entities, such as pathways or regulons. We show that TOSICA achieves fast and accurate one-stop annotation and batch-insensitive integration while providing biologically interpretable insights for understanding cellular behavior during development and disease progressions. We demonstrate TOSICA's advantages by applying it to scRNA-seq data of tumor-infiltrating immune cells, and CD14+ monocytes in COVID-19 to reveal rare cell types, heterogeneity and dynamic trajectories associated with disease progression and severity.

papers.title: Folding non-homologous proteins by coupling deep-learning contact maps with I-TASSER assembly simulations
papers.abstract: Structure prediction for proteins lacking homologous templates in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) remains a significant unsolved problem. We developed a protocol, C-I-TASSER, to integrate interresidue contact maps from deep neural-network learning with the cutting-edge I-TASSER fragment assembly simulations. Large-scale benchmark tests showed that C-I-TASSER can fold more than twice the number of non-homologous proteins than the I-TASSER, which does not use contacts. When applied to a folding experiment on 8,266 unsolved Pfam families, C-I-TASSER successfully folded 4,162 domain families, including 504 folds that are not found in the PDB. Furthermore, it created correct folds for 85% of proteins in the SARS-CoV-2 genome, despite the quick mutation rate of the virus and sparse sequence profiles. The results demonstrated the critical importance of coupling whole-genome and metagenome-based evolutionary information with optimal structure assembly simulations for solving the problem of non-homologous protein structure prediction.

papers.title: CRISCross: Integration of Epigenetic Information for Deep-Learning-Based Prediction of CRISPR-Cas9 Off-Targets Across Cell Types
papers.abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 enables precise genome editing but remains limited by off-target effects, raising safety concerns and necessitating accurate prediction. Although epigenetic features influence Cas9 binding and cleavage, their predictive signals are often weak, highlyvariable, and context-dependent, limiting the effectiveness of existing machine learning approaches. Cross-cell-type settings are especially challenging: epigenetic landscapes differ substantially, and models trained on one cell type frequently fail to generalize. Here, we systematically investigate the role of epigenetic context in off-target prediction and demonstrate that its utility depends on modeling interactions with sequence features rather than treating it as an independent signal. Tabular and deep learning experiments demonstrate that epigenetic features provide a consistent but modestly complementary signal, and that late-stage fusion strategies are insufficient to effectively exploit this information. To address this, we introduce CRISCross, a cross-attention-based architecture that captures sequence-epigenetic interactions at the nucleotide level, alongside CRISPRAT, a synthetic pretraining strategy that learns transferable representations from genome-derived sgRNA-off-target pairs without relying on dataset-specific pretraining. CRISCross, incorporating AlphaGenome-derived chromatin accessibility signals, shows better predictive performance than sequence-only baselines across three independent test datasets spanning two cell types, demonstrating improved generalization across guide RNAs, datasets, and cellular contexts. This is particularly relevant for therapeutic applications involving cell types or patient-derived contexts that lack dedicated experimental datasets. In such settings, predicted chromatin accessibility may provide scalable contextual information when direct epigenomic profiling is unavailable or impractical. Together, these results show that accurate CRISPR off-target prediction benefits from interaction-aware integration of epigenetic context alongside generalizable pretraining strategies.

papers.title: Fine-tuned Medical Vision-Language Model (MedGemma 1.5 4B) with and without Structured Radiologist Descriptors versus EU-TIRADS for Malignancy Risk Stratification of Thyroid Nodules at Ultrasound: A Tunisian Multicenter Diagnostic Accuracy Study
papers.abstract: Purpose. To evaluate a medical vision-language foundation model fine-tuned on thyroid ultrasound images, with or without the radiologist's structured descriptors, against expert-rated EU-TIRADS for the classification of thyroid nodules as benign or malignant. Materials and Methods. This retrospective study included nodules that underwent ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) between January 2019 and August 2025 in two Tunisian centers, with consecutive recruitment, together with a selection of images from an international public dataset. Of 1,580 nodules, 1,456 (272 malignant; 1,280 patients) with an interpretable cytological or histological reference standard were allocated at patient level to training (n = 942), validation (n = 258) and a test set sealed before training (n = 256; 51 malignant). MedGemma 1.5 4B was fine-tuned with low-rank adaptation under four input configurations: the image with nodule biometry, with or without age and sex (A, B); A with chain-of-thought supervision (C); and A plus the eleven qualitative descriptors of the radiologist's structured report (D). The EU-TIRADS category was never a model input. Areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) were compared with DeLong's test and a prespecified non-inferiority margin of 0.05; EU-TIRADS >= 4 was the prespecified comparator, with >= 5 as a sensitivity analysis. Results. Config D reached an AUROC of 0.953 (95% CI 0.909-0.976), versus 0.948 (0.894-0.972) for EU-TIRADS (difference +0.004, 95% CI -0.016 to +0.025), which met the non-inferiority criterion; Configs A-C, without the qualitative descriptors, reached 0.883-0.892 (Holm-adjusted p = 0.045 versus EU-TIRADS). At >= 4, EU-TIRADS had a sensitivity of 98.0% and produced 94 false positives among 205 benign nodules; at a threshold fixed on validation data, Config D reclassified 72 of them as negative while missing two additional cancers. Against EU-TIRADS >= 5 (sensitivity 92.2%, specificity 95.1%), Config D at its native threshold (88.2%, 94.1%) did not classify more nodules correctly (McNemar p = 0.22), and at its two other thresholds it classified fewer nodules correctly (p = 0.004 and 0.007). Raw probabilities were miscalibrated (expected calibration error 0.117 for Config D), and Platt scaling within the test set reduced this error to 0.019-0.040. Conclusion. Given the ultrasound image together with the radiologist's structured descriptors, the fine-tuned model matched expert EU-TIRADS discrimination and, against the >= 4 threshold, reclassified most false positives as negative, a gain concentrated in category 4 and based on only three cancers in category 4. It is best positioned as a report-standardizing second reader in the EU-TIRADS 4 gray zone, pending prospective external validation.

papers.title: Deep learning applications in single-cell genomics and transcriptomics data analysis
papers.abstract: Traditional bulk sequencing methods are limited to measuring the average signal in a group of cells, potentially masking heterogeneity, and rare populations. The single-cell resolution, however, enhances our understanding of complex biological systems and diseases, such as cancer, the immune system, and chronic diseases. However, the single-cell technologies generate massive amounts of data that are often high-dimensional, sparse, and complex, thus making analysis with traditional computational approaches difficult and unfeasible. To tackle these challenges, many are turning to deep learning (DL) methods as potential alternatives to the conventional machine learning (ML) algorithms for single-cell studies. DL is a branch of ML capable of extracting high-level features from raw inputs in multiple stages. Compared to traditional ML, DL models have provided significant improvements across many domains and applications. In this work, we examine DL applications in genomics, transcriptomics, spatial transcriptomics, and multi-omics integration, and address whether DL techniques will prove to be advantageous or if the single-cell omics domain poses unique challenges. Through a systematic literature review, we have found that DL has not yet revolutionized the most pressing challenges of the single-cell omics field. However, using DL models for single-cell omics has shown promising results (in many cases outperforming the previous state-of-the-art models) in data preprocessing and downstream analysis. Although developments of DL algorithms for single-cell omics have generally been gradual, recent advances reveal that DL can offer valuable resources in fast-tracking and advancing research in single-cell.

papers.title: Efficient evolution of human antibodies from general protein language models
papers.abstract: Abstract Natural evolution must explore a vast landscape of possible sequences for desirable yet rare mutations, suggesting that learning from natural evolutionary strategies could guide artificial evolution. Here we report that general protein language models can efficiently evolve human antibodies by suggesting mutations that are evolutionarily plausible, despite providing the model with no information about the target antigen, binding specificity or protein structure. We performed language-model-guided affinity maturation of seven antibodies, screening 20 or fewer variants of each antibody across only two rounds of laboratory evolution, and improved the binding affinities of four clinically relevant, highly mature antibodies up to sevenfold and three unmatured antibodies up to 160-fold, with many designs also demonstrating favorable thermostability and viral neutralization activity against Ebola and severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) pseudoviruses. The same models that improve antibody binding also guide efficient evolution across diverse protein families and selection pressures, including antibiotic resistance and enzyme activity, suggesting that these results generalize to many settings.

papers.title: THItoGene: a deep learning method for predicting spatial transcriptomics from histological images
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics unveils the complex dynamics of cell regulation and transcriptomes, but it is typically cost-prohibitive. Predicting spatial gene expression from histological images via artificial intelligence offers a more affordable option, yet existing methods fall short in extracting deep-level information from pathological images. In this paper, we present THItoGene, a hybrid neural network that utilizes dynamic convolutional and capsule networks to adaptively sense potential molecular signals in histological images for exploring the relationship between high-resolution pathology image phenotypes and regulation of gene expression. A comprehensive benchmark evaluation using datasets from human breast cancer and cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma has demonstrated the superior performance of THItoGene in spatial gene expression prediction. Moreover, THItoGene has demonstrated its capacity to decipher both the spatial context and enrichment signals within specific tissue regions. THItoGene can be freely accessed at https://github.com/yrjia1015/THItoGene.

papers.title: I Asked a ChatGPT to Write an Editorial About How We Can Incorporate Chatbots Into Neurosurgical Research and Patient Care…
papers.abstract: Efforts to apply artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning in the medical field and specifically in neurosurgery are actively underway.1-7 Currently, imaging-based diagnosis, disease diagnosis, and methods of prediction using clinical data and genomic data are fields that receive the most attention.3-6,8-11 However, AI technologies associated with natural language processing are also being investigated.12 Conversational AI is an application of natural language processing that refers to AI technologies capable of communicating with people.13 These include chatbots or virtual agents using generative pretraining transformer (GPT) language models. These technologies are rapidly advancing and are poised to make a significant contribution to medical research and patient care. Multiple groups have already put various conversational AI platforms to use them foradvance patient care including taking down medical histories, assisting in psychotherapy, and improving care in chronic conditions.7,13-16 However, the conventional conversational AI platforms were limited with mostly structured rules of engagement. ChatGPT has new potential roles in both patient care and research including producing primary documents and assisting in research conceptualization/design. We gave a ChatGPT (OpenAI LLC) with the following prompt: Write me a research editorial for the journal: Neurosurgery about how we can incorporate chatbots into neurosurgical research and neurosurgical patient care and received an insightful and well-written correspondence completely generated by the software. We comment on how as a community we need to carefully embrace these powerful technologies to improve neurosurgical research and patient outcomes. “Integrating Chatbot Technology into Neurosurgical Research and Patient Care: A Research Editorial Over the past few years, chatbot technology has made significant strides in the field of health care, with chatbots being used to assist with tasks such as patient education, appointment scheduling, and symptom management. The use of chatbots in neurosurgery is a relatively new area of exploration, but it has the potential to revolutionize the way we conduct research and deliver care to patients with brain and nervous system conditions. One potential application of chatbot technology in neurosurgery is in the field of research. Chatbots can be used to gather data from large numbers of patients, streamlining the process of data collection and analysis. This can be particularly useful in longitudinal studies, where chatbots can be used to track patient outcomes over time. Chatbots can also be used to administer surveys or questionnaires to patients, allowing researchers to gather data on patient experiences and preferences. papers.title: DeepST: identifying spatial domains in spatial transcriptomics by deep learning
papers.abstract: Recent advances in spatial transcriptomics (ST) have brought unprecedented opportunities to understand tissue organization and function in spatial context. However, it is still challenging to precisely dissect spatial domains with similar gene expression and histology in situ. Here, we present DeepST, an accurate and universal deep learning framework to identify spatial domains, which performs better than the existing state-of-the-art methods on benchmarking datasets of the human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Further testing on a breast cancer ST dataset, we showed that DeepST can dissect spatial domains in cancer tissue at a finer scale. Moreover, DeepST can achieve not only effective batch integration of ST data generated from multiple batches or different technologies, but also expandable capabilities for processing other spatial omics data. Together, our results demonstrate that DeepST has the exceptional capacity for identifying spatial domains, making it a desirable tool to gain novel insights from ST studies.

papers.title: Integrated analysis of multimodal single-cell data with structural similarity
papers.abstract: Multimodal single-cell sequencing technologies provide unprecedented information on cellular heterogeneity from multiple layers of genomic readouts. However, joint analysis of two modalities without properly handling the noise often leads to overfitting of one modality by the other and worse clustering results than vanilla single-modality analysis. How to efficiently utilize the extra information from single cell multi-omics to delineate cell states and identify meaningful signal remains as a significant computational challenge. In this work, we propose a deep learning framework, named SAILERX, for efficient, robust, and flexible analysis of multi-modal single-cell data. SAILERX consists of a variational autoencoder with invariant representation learning to correct technical noises from sequencing process, and a multimodal data alignment mechanism to integrate information from different modalities. Instead of performing hard alignment by projecting both modalities to a shared latent space, SAILERX encourages the local structures of two modalities measured by pairwise similarities to be similar. This strategy is more robust against overfitting of noises, which facilitates various downstream analysis such as clustering, imputation, and marker gene detection. Furthermore, the invariant representation learning part enables SAILERX to perform integrative analysis on both multi- and single-modal datasets, making it an applicable and scalable tool for more general scenarios.

papers.title: Efficient prediction of a spatial transcriptomics profile better characterizes breast cancer tissue sections without costly experimentation
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics is an emerging technology requiring costly reagents and considerable skills, limiting the identification of transcriptional markers related to histology. Here, we show that predicted spatial gene-expression in unmeasured regions and tissues can enhance biologists' histological interpretations. We developed the Deep learning model for Spatial gene Clusters and Expression, DeepSpaCE, and confirmed its performance using the spatial-transcriptome profiles and immunohistochemistry images of consecutive human breast cancer tissue sections. For example, the predicted expression patterns of SPARC, an invasion marker, highlighted a small tumor-invasion region difficult to identify using raw spatial transcriptome data alone because of a lack of measurements. We further developed semi-supervised DeepSpaCE using unlabeled histology images and increased the imputation accuracy of consecutive sections, enhancing applicability for a small sample size. Our method enables users to derive hidden histological characters via spatial transcriptome and gene annotations, leading to accelerated biological discoveries without additional experiments.

papers.title: De novo design of protein structure and function with RFdiffusion
papers.abstract: Abstract There has been considerable recent progress in designing new proteins using deep-learning methods 1–9 . Despite this progress, a general deep-learning framework for protein design that enables solution of a wide range of design challenges, including de novo binder design and design of higher-order symmetric architectures, has yet to be described. Diffusion models 10,11 have had considerable success in image and language generative modelling but limited success when applied to protein modelling, probably due to the complexity of protein backbone geometry and sequence–structure relationships. Here we show that by fine-tuning the RoseTTAFold structure prediction network on protein structure denoising tasks, we obtain a generative model of protein backbones that achieves outstanding performance on unconditional and topology-constrained protein monomer design, protein binder design, symmetric oligomer design, enzyme active site scaffolding and symmetric motif scaffolding for therapeutic and metal-binding protein design. We demonstrate the power and generality of the method, called RoseTTAFold diffusion (RFdiffusion), by experimentally characterizing the structures and functions of hundreds of designed symmetric assemblies, metal-binding proteins and protein binders. The accuracy of RFdiffusion is confirmed by the cryogenic electron microscopy structure of a designed binder in complex with influenza haemagglutinin that is nearly identical to the design model. In a manner analogous to networks that produce images from user-specified inputs, RFdiffusion enables the design of diverse functional proteins from simple molecular specifications.
